items.readable_text:
Content:
Fractions that contain multiple terms in the numerator and a single term in the denominator can be split into separate terms.

Content:
For example,

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\dfrac {x + 2} {3} &= \
\dfrac x 3 + \dfrac 2 3
}]

Content:
and

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\dfrac {3a - 4b + 1} {5} &= \
\dfrac {3a} 5 - \dfrac {4b} 5 + \dfrac 1 5.
}]

Content:
Often, we're able to simplify the fractions in the individual terms, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\dfrac {10x + 9} {2} &= \
\dfrac {10x} {2} + \dfrac 9 2 &= \
\dfrac {10} {2} \cdot x + \dfrac 9 2 &= \
5 \cdot x + \dfrac 9 2 &= \
5x + \dfrac 9 2
}]

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: \dfrac{6y − 1}{3} = ay + b,] what are the values of [MATH: a] and [MATH: b?]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: \dfrac{6y − 1}{3} = ay + b,] what are the values of [MATH: a] and [MATH: b?]

sections.normalized_html:
Splitting the fraction into separate terms and then simplifying the fractions in the individual terms, we get

[MATH: \eqalign{ \dfrac{6y − 1}{3} &= \ \dfrac{6y}{3} - \dfrac 1 3 &= \ \dfrac{6}{3} \cdot y - \dfrac 1 3 &= \ 2 \cdot y - \dfrac 1 3 &= \ 2y - \dfrac 1 3 &. }]

Writing the above in the form [MATH: ay+b,] we get

[MATH: (2)_(⏟)_(a)y + (− (1)/(3))_(⏟)_(b).]

Therefore, [MATH: a=2] and [MATH: b=-\dfrac{1}{3}.]

[MATH: ((1)/(4))_(⏟)_(p) + (− (1)/(2))_(⏟)_(q)a + (4)_(⏟)_(r)b.]

Therefore, [MATH: p=\dfrac{1}{4},] [MATH: q=-\dfrac{1}{2},] and [MATH: r=4.]
